title: Redwood Discovery - Meridian Banking latency & throughput discussion
summary: Discovery call to understand Meridian's p95 latency & throughput targets for LLM features across customer support and fraud detection. Discussed concurrency, token/sec expectations, streaming, benchmark design, and security needs (VPC, KMS, SOC2). Agreed to run a token/sec + p95 benchmark with sample prompts and share price/commit options for Dedicated.
next_steps: Jordan to send benchmark template and cost/commit options (by 2026-03-06)
Priya to share sample prompt set and expected concurrency patterns (by 2026-03-09)
Sana to schedule a dedicated technical deep-dive with infra team to scope VPC/on-prem options (week of 2026-03-16)
action_items: Jordan Kim: Share benchmark spreadsheet, draft SLO doc, and Redwood security brief (due 2026-03-06)
Priya Singh: Provide representative prompt set and traffic histogram (due 2026-03-09)
Tom Hollis: Gather questions for SOC2/KMS integration and send to Sana (due 2026-03-10)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 mins
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Sana (Redwood SE), Luca (Redwood SE), Alex (Meridian), Priya (Meridian), Tom (Meridian), Mei (Meridian)

[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick roll call?
[00:04] Alex Ortega: Alex here, hi.
[00:06] Priya Singh: Priya here.
[00:08] Tom Hollis: Tom.
[00:09] Mei Chen: Mei.
[00:12] Jordan Kim: Great thanks. Agenda: understand your p95 targets and throughput for the features you mentioned — customer support triage and realtime fraud signals — and figure out hosted vs dedicated vs private. Sana will jump into benchmarks and infra details.
[00:25] Sana Patel: Hey all, quick overview — Redwood hosted works well for teams starting up, Dedicated is reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and Private (VPC/on-prem) for regulated stuff. For the kind of p95s you mentioned we usually benchmark token/sec and p95 over a mix of prompt lengths.
[00:40] Priya Singh: For us, target p95 is 250-300ms for short prompts in support flow, that's for single-turn completions with streaming enabled ideally. For fraud detection secondary model calls we can tolerate 700ms p95 but need higher throughput, like 200 concurrent requests, each ~60 tokens.
[00:58] Jordan Kim: Got it. So 250-300ms p95 for short support prompts with streaming, and 700ms p95 for fraud with concurrency ~200, tokens ~60. Roughly what's your token/sec expectation?
[01:10] Priya Singh: For support we see bursts up to 1200 tokens/sec cluster-wide, sustained maybe 400 tokens/sec during peak. Fraud workload is burstier, maybe 12k tokens/sec when scoring batches, but often it's many concurrent small requests so latency matters.
[01:28] Luca Moreno: A couple clarifying q's — when you say streaming for support, is it full token-by-token UX or chunked streaming? That changes per-request footprint.
[01:37] Priya Singh: Ideally token-by-token, yes. The UI renders as they come so we prefer streaming. But we can do small chunked streaming if that helps.
[01:45] Alex Ortega: Also want to confirm data residency — production data must live in our VPC in us-east-1 and keys managed by our KMS/HSM.
[01:53] Sana Patel: Totally, we support customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated options integrate with KMS for key wrapping. Hosted has bring-your-own-key in certain regions — we can map out specifics.
[02:05] Tom Hollis: SOC2 and audit logs are mandatory, plus SAML SSO and RBAC.
[02:10] Jordan Kim: Yep those are standard asks. We'll include our SOC2 report and logging examples in the security brief.
[02:16] Sana Patel: On the perf side, we typically test models with sequence profiles: short (<=64 tokens), medium (~256 tokens), long (~1024 tokens) and measure p95, p50 and token/sec at target concurrency. For streaming we measure time-to-first-byte and p95 time-per-chunk which matters for UX.
[02:34] Priya Singh: Can you give an example of what Dedicated looks like for 200 concurrency? Like GPU counts, batching sizes, and expected token/sec?
[02:42] Luca Moreno: Sure, ballpark — for a 70B dense model on A100-class GPUs, sustaining 200 concurrent small requests with ~60 tokens each might need a pool of 6-8 GPUs with continuous batching tuned; token/sec depends on batching efficiency but you'd be in the few thousands tokens/sec per pool. For quantized or smaller models that drops. This is fuzzy — we should run a benchmark with your exact prompts.
[03:05] Alex Ortega: Ok yeah we need exact numbers. Our infra is sensitive to cost so we'd compare Hosted cost vs Dedicated monthly commit.
[03:12] Jordan Kim: We'll provide cost estimates for hosted per-token and for dedicated commit tiers — and show where streaming increases egress/cost. Also note caching and automatic prefix KV cache can reduce token cost especially for repeated prompts.
[03:26] Mei Chen: Quick Q — how much does KV cache actually help for support, since we have lots of repeated opening prompts?
[03:31] Sana Patel: If prompts share prefixes a lot, KV cache can save up to 60-70% token compute on repeated calls in our experience. But depends on prompt diversity.
[03:40] Priya Singh: For fraud we can't really cache due to unique transaction context.
[03:44] Sana Patel: Right, fraud is usually low cache hit.
[03:47] Tom Hollis: For private deployment we need the full control plane in our environment or at least a VPC peering with audit log egress control. Are there air-gapped options?
[03:55] Jordan Kim: Yes — Private offers customer-controlled network with on-prem packaging for air-gapped regs. That path includes integration work and separate SLA. We'll scope in the deep-dive.
[04:04] Alex Ortega: On benchmarking — what's the best way to run token/sec tests? We can spin up a load generator but want Redwood to run something comparable to our production pattern.
[04:12] Luca Moreno: We usually run a distributed runner that replays your traffic histogram against the target model variants. We'll measure p95 on the tail and tokens/sec per GPU/pool. We'll need your sample prompts and a traffic histogram — Priya you mentioned that?
[04:25] Priya Singh: Yes we'll share. We'll anonymize payloads.
[04:28] Jordan Kim: Great. Also worth noting: streaming adds some overhead on small requests because of chunking and network hops; time-to-first-byte often determines perceived latency more than total completion time.
[04:39] Priya Singh: For support UX we care most about time-to-first-token under 150-200ms ideally. Is that achievable on hosted?
[04:47] Sana Patel: For short prompts on hosted with our optimized kernels and regional routing it's often possible to hit 150-200ms p50 and p95 in the low 200s depending on model choice; with Dedicated/Pinned GPUs you can get more predictable low p95s. We'll show model-level profiles in the benchmark.
[05:03] Alex Ortega: Any gotchas on tokenization differences or prompt length accounting for pricing? We use a lot of code snippets and multi-lingual content.
[05:10] Jordan Kim: We'll include tokenizer parity notes and sample token counts for your prompt set. Pricing is per token as usual but we'll show real effective token cost after caching and batching.
[05:18] Mei Chen: For concurrency are you suggesting vertical autoscale or more horizontal pools?
[05:22] Luca Moreno: We generally do pool-based GPU autoscaling with configurable burst capacity; Dedicated gives you reserved pools plus autoscale policies, hosted is multi-tenant so slightly different guarantees.
[05:33] Priya Singh: Ok next question: if we run with streaming enabled, do we lose batching efficiency?
[05:38] Sana Patel: Streaming can limit some batching — token-by-token streaming reduces batching window; but we support hybrid strategies: small chunk streaming and protocol optimizations to keep batching efficiency high. It's a tradeoff between latency and throughput. We'll show measured impact in the bench.
[05:54] Tom Hollis: Security again — will the benchmark data touch Redwood's hosted env if we run tests there? We need assurances about ephemeral data handling and logs.
[06:03] Jordan Kim: For hosted benchmarks we can sign an NDA and use anonymized samples; logs and payloads can be configured to be ephemeral and not persisted. For Dedicated/Private the data stays in your VPC and keys under your KMS if you prefer.
[06:16] Alex Ortega: Great. Anything else operational — SLOs, retry/backoff patterns?
[06:21] Luca Moreno: We recommend client-side retries with exponential backoff, idempotency keys for non-repeatable ops, and circuit-breakers for graceful degradation. Redwood supports route-level fallbacks to smaller model variants to keep latency under SLOs if capacity constrained.
[06:37] Priya Singh: That fallback story is interesting — we'd rather degrade gracefully to a cheaper model than spike latency.
[06:42] Sana Patel: Exactly — canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies are part of Redwood Optimize and Console features.
[06:50] Jordan Kim: Ok let's recap and assign next steps. We will: 1) Send the benchmark template & security brief; 2) Run an initial hosted micro-benchmark with anonymized prompts if you want, and 3) Schedule a technical deep-dive for Private/VPC scope.
[07:05] Priya Singh: Sounds good. We'll share prompt sets and traffic histograms.
[07:08] Alex Ortega: We'll also compile a short list of models to evaluate, and cost sensitivity thresholds.
[07:12] Tom Hollis: I'll review the SOC2 docs and send any further compliance Qs.
[07:15] Jordan Kim: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the deep-dive.
[07:19] Mei Chen: Thanks all.
[07:21] Jordan Kim: End call.

Notes on transcription: occasional word swaps (e.g., "KV cash" vs KV cache), minor filler words and cross talk.
